newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares end lower in lacklustre trade.
newsitem.headline: India shares end lower in lacklustre trade.

text.p: Indian blue chips drifted lower on Monday, capping early gains as buyers stayed on the sidelines awaiting a possible oil price hike, dealers said.
Activity was concentrated in second-tier stocks, with increased investment buying seen in many software, bank and state-run firms, they said.
"There is a total shift of action from blue chips to smaller stocks due to cheap valuations," said R. Ramakrishnan, chief dealer at ASK-Raymond James Securities Ltd in Bombay.
"These (second-tier) stocks have seen investment and fund buying," Ramakrishnan said.
The nagging worry of a hike in government-set oil prices was worrying markets, dealers said. "The uncertainty over the timing of the hike has unsettled the market," said a local dealer.
Analysts expect the government to raise prices of petroleum products to partially offset a 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) deficit in the oil-pool account, which is hurting oil refiners.
India imports most of its oil but sells to domestic consumers at below world prices through a complex cross-subsidy system. The price difference is funded by the oil-pool account.
Lack of follow-up buying at current levels posed a hurdle for the market to add onto its gains, players said.
"The market closed on a weak note. Nobody is confident that prices will sustain at higher levels," said Purvesh Shah, chief dealer at Nucleus Securities.
The approval on Friday of a business-friendly budget for 1997/98 (April-March) was largely discounted, traders said.
Indian parliament approved the budget with its tax and tariff cuts intact, after being held hostage to political developments since its presentation on February 28.
"There is still a lot of room to go up, but the market will not run away," Nirmal Jain, managing director at Probity Research & Services, said.
